The technique enables instructions to be delivered efficiently to multiple workers located at different positions within the same space. The instruction device includes a feature point detector, a marker information storage unit, an inter-image transformation parameter calculator, and a marker information transformer.

The feature point detector acquires images captured from first and second viewpoints and identifies corresponding feature points in those images. The marker information storage unit stores positional information for a marker superimposed on the image captured from the first viewpoint. Using the detected feature points, the inter-image transformation parameter calculator determines the transformation parameters that describe the spatial relationship between the two images. The marker information transformer then applies the calculated transformation to the marker position in the first image, thereby determining the corresponding marker position in the image captured from the second viewpoint.

By transforming marker information between images captured from different viewpoints, the device can present consistent, location-relevant instructions to workers throughout the space.
outputs.L4:
An instruction device provides appropriate guidance to multiple workers operating at different positions in a shared work area. The device acquires a first image of the work area from a first viewpoint and a second image from a different viewpoint. It detects corresponding feature points in the two images, such as corners, edges, patterns, or other visually identifiable portions of objects in the environment. Based on these correspondences, the device calculates transformation parameters that describe the positional relationship between the first and second images.

When an instruction marker is placed at a designated position in the first image, the device applies the calculated transformation parameters to determine the corresponding position in the second image. The marker may identify, for example, a component to be handled, a location at which an operation is to be performed, or a direction in which an object should be moved. The transformed marker can then be superimposed on or otherwise associated with the second image so that the same instruction is presented correctly from the second worker’s viewpoint.

This approach allows instructions created with reference to one image to be reused for workers viewing the work area from other positions. Each worker can therefore receive guidance aligned with that worker’s own perspective, reducing confusion caused by differences in viewing direction, scale, or position. By automatically converting instruction locations between viewpoints, the device supports efficient coordination and accurate task execution without requiring separate instructions to be manually prepared for every worker.

### The Power of “The”

“The” is one of the smallest and most frequently used words in the English language. Known as the definite article, it points to a specific person, place, object, or idea. For example, “a book” can mean any book, while “the book” refers to one that is already known or clearly identified.

Although it often goes unnoticed, “the” gives language precision and context. It helps speakers distinguish between something general and something particular. This simple word demonstrates how even the shortest elements of language can play an essential role in communication.

The device detects feature points or feature regions in the first and second images, establishes correspondences between the detected features, and determines inter-image transformation parameters based on the correspondences. The device receives or identifies one or more marker positions in the first image and transforms the marker positions into corresponding positions in the second image using the inter-image transformation parameters. The transformed marker positions may be corrected based on local feature matching, image geometry, or confidence information and output for display, annotation, measurement, navigation, or subsequent image processing. Thus, marker information can be transferred between differently viewed images without requiring manual repositioning of each marker.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a technical description of a system that maps an augmented-reality marker from a first camera image to a second viewpoint.
counterfactuals.output:
## System for Mapping an Augmented-Reality Marker Between Viewpoints

The system maps an augmented-reality (AR) marker detected in an image captured from a first viewpoint into the image coordinate system of a second viewpoint. The system includes a first camera, a second camera or virtual camera, a processing unit, and a calibration data store containing intrinsic and extrinsic camera parameters.

A marker detector processes a first image to identify the marker and determine image coordinates for a set of marker features, such as its four corners. If the marker’s physical dimensions and geometry are known, the system associates the detected image features with corresponding points in a marker-local coordinate system. Using the first camera’s intrinsic calibration, the system estimates the six-degree-of-freedom pose of the marker relative to the first camera. The pose may be represented by a rotation matrix \(R_{1m}\) and translation vector \(t_{1m}\), satisfying

\[
X_1 = R_{1m}X_m + t_{1m},
\]

where \(X_m\) is a point in marker coordinates and \(X_1\) is the corresponding three-dimensional point in the first camera coordinate system.

The system obtains the rigid transformation between the first and second viewpoints. This transformation may be determined by stereo calibration, camera tracking, visual-inertial odometry, simultaneous localization and mapping, or a known virtual-camera configuration. If the transformation from the first camera frame to the second camera frame is represented by \(R_{21}\) and \(t_{21}\), the marker pose in the second camera frame is computed as

\[
R_{2m}=R_{21}R_{1m},
\]

\[
t_{2m}=R_{21}t_{1m}+t_{21}.
\]

Each marker point is then transformed into the second camera frame:

\[
X_2 = R_{2m}X_m+t_{2m}.
\]

Using the intrinsic calibration matrix \(K_2\) of the second camera, the transformed point is projected into the second image:

\[
\tilde{x}_2 = K_2X_2,
\qquad
x_2 =
\begin{bmatrix}
\tilde{x}_2^{(1)}/\tilde{x}_2^{(3)} \\
\tilde{x}_2^{(2)}/\tilde{x}_2^{(3)}
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Lens distortion may be applied after projection, or input images may be rectified before processing. Points having non-positive depth in the second camera frame are rejected. The resulting projected corner coordinates define the marker’s location, scale, orientation, and perspective distortion as viewed from the second viewpoint.

For a planar marker, the mapping may alternatively be represented by a homography. Given the marker pose relative to the second camera, the plane-to-image homography is

\[
H_2 = K_2
\begin{bmatrix}
r_1 & r_2 & t_{2m}
\end{bmatrix},
\]

where \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) are the first two columns of \(R_{2m}\). A texture, annotation, or other AR content defined in marker-plane coordinates can be warped into the second image using \(H_2\).

If the physical marker geometry is unknown, a direct image-to-image homography may be estimated from matched coplanar features in the two views. For nonplanar content, or where viewpoint translation produces significant parallax, the system instead uses reconstructed depth, a three-dimensional marker model, or a spatial map; a single homography is not sufficient.

The processing unit may also calculate a confidence value based on marker-detection quality, reprojection error, calibration uncertainty, viewpoint separation, and occlusion. Temporal filtering may be applied to the estimated marker pose to reduce jitter. Before rendering, the system may perform field-of-view clipping, depth-based occlusion testing, and visibility checks so that the mapped marker or associated AR content is composited consistently into the second viewpoint.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain how an instruction device comprising a feature point detector (1501), marker information storage unit (1500), inter-image transformation parameter calculator (1504), and marker information transformer (1505) operates.
counterfactuals.output:
The instruction device updates marker information so that it remains aligned with a target object or scene as images change.

1. **Marker information storage unit (1500)**  
   Stores marker data associated with a reference image or an earlier captured image. The data may include the marker’s position, shape, orientation, boundary, or coordinates of instruction points.

2. **Feature point detector (1501)**  
   Detects distinctive feature points—such as corners, edges, or texture points—in the reference image and in a newly acquired image. Corresponding feature points are matched between the two images.

3. **Inter-image transformation parameter calculator (1504)**  
   Uses the matched feature points to calculate parameters describing the geometric relationship between the images. Depending on the application, this may be a translation, rotation, scaling, affine transformation, or projective transformation/homography. Outlier correspondences may be rejected to improve accuracy.

4. **Marker information transformer (1505)**  
   Applies the calculated transformation to the stored marker coordinates or geometry. The transformed marker information is then appropriate for the new image.

Thus, if the camera or target moves, the device automatically relocates and reshapes the stored marker so that an instruction—such as an arrow, highlight, work area, or guidance symbol—continues to appear at the correct position in the current image.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate patent claim-style text for technology that calculates an image-to-image transformation and converts marker positional information so the marker can be superimposed correctly on a second image.
counterfactuals.output:
1. **A computer-implemented image processing method comprising:**  
   acquiring a first image and a second image depicting at least partially overlapping subject matter;  
   calculating an image-to-image transformation that maps coordinates in a coordinate system of the first image to corresponding coordinates in a coordinate system of the second image;  
   obtaining marker positional information identifying a position of a marker relative to the first image;  
   converting the marker positional information, using the image-to-image transformation, into transformed marker positional information relative to the second image; and  
   generating display data in which the marker is superimposed on the second image at a position specified by the transformed marker positional information.

2. **The method of claim 1**, wherein calculating the image-to-image transformation comprises detecting corresponding feature points in the first image and the second image and estimating the image-to-image transformation based on the corresponding feature points.

3. **The method of claim 1**, wherein the image-to-image transformation comprises at least one of a translation, a rotation, a scaling transformation, an affine transformation, a projective transformation, a homography, or a non-rigid transformation.

4. **The method of claim 1**, wherein the marker positional information comprises at least one of a point coordinate, a bounding region, a contour, a line, a polygon, or a segmentation mask.

5. **The method of claim 1**, further comprising determining a confidence value associated with the image-to-image transformation and superimposing the marker on the second image in response to the confidence value satisfying a threshold.

6. **The method of claim 1**, wherein generating the display data comprises adjusting at least one of a size, orientation, shape, or perspective of the marker according to the image-to-image transformation.

7. **The method of claim 1**, wherein the first image and the second image are acquired at different times, from different viewpoints, using different imaging devices, or using different imaging modalities.

8. **An image processing system comprising:**  
   one or more processors; and  
   memory storing instructions that, when executed by the one or more processors, cause the image processing system to:  
   calculate a transformation between a first image and a second image;  
   receive positional information defining a marker with respect to the first image;  
   transform the positional information into a coordinate system of the second image using the transformation; and  
   cause the marker to be superimposed on the second image in accordance with the transformed positional information.

9. **The image processing system of claim 8**, wherein the instructions further cause the image processing system to update the transformed positional information in response to movement, resizing, or deformation of the second image.

10. **A non-transitory computer-readable medium** storing instructions that, when executed by one or more processors, cause the one or more processors to perform the method of any one of claims 1-7.
